extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers of scientific method, experimentalists, and philosophers of science
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and evaluation of the four experimental methods of induction (Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations, Residues) and associated precautions for drawing causal inferences from empirical data. Includes examples (poisons, motion, electricity, dew) that illustrate application limits and required controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: When A changes in quantity and a also changes in quantity so that a numerical relation between their changes can be traced within our limits of observation, we may (with precautions) conclude the same numerical relation will hold beyond those limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires knowledge of how A and a vary together (absolute quantities preferred). Examples: determining whether an effect scales proportionally with a cause (e.g., if A doubles and a doubles). Use to estimate the fraction of effect attributable to the cause when other independent causes exist. Apply cautiously: know total quantities when possible; check for counteracting causes; beware narrow observational ranges where different laws produce similar results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of knowing absolute quantities before inferring numerical relations
rubrics_metrics.description: If we do not know the total (absolute) quantities of antecedent and consequent, we cannot determine the real numerical relation according to which those quantities vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: concluding an effect is wholly due to a cause (e.g., assuming complete contraction of particle distances if heat were exhausted) without knowing absolute heat or true particle spacing. Practical implication: when aiming to infer proportional or functional relations, measure absolute magnitudes or acknowledge limits of inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility of counteracting or novel causes beyond observed limits
rubrics_metrics.description: There is always the possibility that beyond observed limits some counteracting cause, new agent, or dormant property may develop and alter the law of variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This risk limits extrapolation: conclusions from concomitant variations cannot be considered complete inductions for conditions outside observed ranges. Account for potential new agents or changed properties when predicting outside empirical bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger from narrow observational ranges (mathematical indistinguishability of laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the extreme limits of observation are very narrow compared to possible variations, very different laws of variation may produce numerical results that differ only slightly within those limits, producing a risk of misidentifying the true law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-relying on formulae or empirical laws derived from narrow ranges (Herschel's examples: elasticity of steam, resistance of fluids). Seek broader variation where possible; quantify uncertainty in extrapolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference (strict form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare positive and negative cases which are as similar as possible except for one antecedent; if the effect occurs when the antecedent is present and does not occur when it is absent (all else equal), that antecedent is a cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigor requires the positive and negative instances to differ only in the single circumstance hypothesised as causal. Examples: using antidotes that prevent a poison from combining with tissues to show the chemical combination is the proximate cause of death. Anti-pattern: using cases that differ in many respects; then inference is unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect Method of Difference / Joint Method of Agreement and Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: When strict Method of Difference cannot be realized, combine Agreement and Difference indirectly: show many different substances share a single property correlated with the effect, and when that property is removed (or counteracted) the effect is absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides strong but not absolutely complete evidence — can approach the rigor of Difference arbitrarily closely when many independent instances share only the one relevant property (e.g., multiple antidotes all form insoluble compounds with poisons). Still beware remaining untested shared properties and alternative explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: If multiple instances that produce the same effect all share a single antecedent (and do not consistently share other circumstances), that antecedent is a candidate for the proximate cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as initial identification of possible causes (example: metallic compounds combining with tissues and preventing putrefaction correlates with death by metallic poisons). Agreement alone cannot determine direction (cause vs effect) and must be tested by Difference or other methods; treat Agreement as hypothesis-generating rather than conclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues (qualified)
rubrics_metrics.description: A method for assigning portions of a complex effect to different antecedents by subtracting known causes and attributing the remainder (residue) to the remaining antecedent(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes Method of Residues is not independent of deduction and requires specific experience; include it among methods of direct observation and experiment but use deduction to support its application. (Detailed application examples are not given in this chunk.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary abstraction and precise definition of the phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: Before attempting causal analysis, precisely determine what the phenomenon is (separate it from other similar phenomena) and limit the term to the intended occurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: define 'dew' clearly (distinct from rain, fog, or visible wet) before investigating causes. This preliminary operation is essential for correct application of Agreement and Difference methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collecting negative/contrary cases and varying circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: To apply the Method of Difference one must collect instances where the phenomenon is absent and vary circumstances to identify which differences correlate with absence of the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (dew): compare surfaces that dew and those that do not (polished metals vs glass); if multiple negative cases share only one lacking quality, that quality becomes the candidate cause. Use controlled variation (e.g., expose polished surfaces of many kinds) to isolate the property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that Difference instances differ only by the single tested quality of the substance
rubrics_metrics.description: In substance-comparison experiments (e.g., dew on glass vs polished metal), the ideal is that substances compared differ solely in the specific quality suspected to be causal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical step: vary the substance alone as much as possible (polished surfaces of varying materials) to ensure the only commonality among dewed surfaces is the suspected quality. Beware manifold differences among materials which can confound inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration across multiple methods strengthens causal claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When the same conclusion is supported by different methods (Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations) the causal inference is much stronger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the mutual necessity and quantitative limitation of opposite electricities is supported by Agreement (various electrification cases), Difference (Leyden jar behaviour), and Concomitant Variations (capacity of neighbouring bodies limits charge). Still examine special-cases (Faraday's voltaic-wire experiment) that reveal important nuances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of internal accommodation or alternative loci for required concomitants
rubrics_metrics.description: A case that appears to be a counterexample to a rule (e.g., induction of opposite electricity) may be explained by the required concomitant being contained internally rather than in a neighbouring body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in voltaic circuits the two opposite currents may be accommodated within the same wire, so no induced current appears in a neighbouring wire — this shows the need to consider the physical locus and capacity of potential concomitants when applying Agreement/Difference reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit of proof to observed extreme limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions from concomitant variations can be regarded as proved only for cases that fall between the same extreme limits of variation which were observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not claim universal applicability beyond observed extremes. You may be assured the observed relation holds within the observed extremes, but not necessarily beyond them without further evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of the Composition of Causes (general rule of causation)
rubrics_metrics.description: More of the cause is followed by more of the effect (composition of causes), except in special cases where causes change properties when conjoined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat this as a general heuristic for causal expectation (used to motivate concomitant variation thinking), but remain alert to exceptional cases where causes interact and change properties when combined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of deduction as auxiliary to experimental methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction (via the four methods) is assisted by deduction; both together compose the available resources for ascertaining laws of succession of phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply deductive reasoning to analyze results from Agreement/Difference/Concomitant Variations/Residues, to design decisive tests, and to integrate experimental findings into broader theoretical frameworks.
